changes.change: Two fixes: (a) Extracted _seed_facts_once() + _ensure_seeded() lazy-init guard. The startup event is unreliable in TestClient, so /api/facts now calls _ensure_seeded() to guarantee the seed runs on first read. (b) POST /api/facts now uses FactCreate (the 3-field input model) instead of Fact (the 7-field full model) so the client does not have to send server-assigned fields.

Removed reset_registry() + the 3-fact re-seed from Orchestrator.__init__. Previously the orchestrator was constructed on every /api/orchestrator/process HTTP request, so every request was wiping the in-memory facts and re-seeding with a different Technical statement. The orchestrator now leaves the facts registry alone; seeding belongs to the app startup only.

Added 2 regression tests: (1) test_orchestrator_does_not_wipe_operator_facts -- POSTs a unique-marked fact, calls /api/orchestrator/process, asserts the fact is still there. Verified the test catches the old bug by manual replay. (2) test_evaluation_suite_is_deterministic -- runs /api/eval/run 3 times, strips runId+timestamp (the only non-deterministic fields), asserts the rest is byte-identical. Closes OPEN_ITEMS B2.

payload.description: The Tauri shell, third_party_assistant.py REPL, discovery_agent, monitor_agent, and InventoryAgent were never run end-to-end against each other. D5 wires them into a single user-facing flow using Ollama tool calling -- the operator types a natural-language question and a local LLM (aegis 1.5B Qwen2) loops over tool calls to the FastAPI audit server until it has an answer.
design_notes: The Ollama Python package was NOT added to requirements.txt. The REPL uses urllib.request, which is stdlib and already used elsewhere in the project.
The 9 tool functions are all wrappers around FastAPI endpoints. The REPL does NOT import from src/engines or src/agents directly -- same boundary rule tests/ follows.
A small Ollama schema builder (_ollama_schema) parses each function docstring for Google-style Args: sections. Avoids the ollama Python package and pydantic.
The live end-to-end test is skip-guarded with executable documentation (the skip message names the exact host feature missing).
third_party_assistant.py chat command spawns the REPL as a subprocess rather than importing it. This keeps the REPL out of the runtime import graph entirely.

grade.post_state: All 7 real issues closed. The script is now USB-deployable: the install path is derived from the script own location; the script refuses to run on Python < 3.12; pip failures mark the deploy DEGRADED (not COMPLETE); launchers are templated from $InstallPath; the closing step re-derives the Merkle chain and prints MATCH/BROKEN.
grade.pre_state: 10 issues found; 7 of them real. Top: hardcoded C:\OrderGetItRight install path, no Python version check, no verify_chain after deploy, launchers hardcoded install path, no project-root marker check.

1_no_ambient_state.change: Step 0a now refuses to run unless pyproject.toml AND 02_Technical\ exist in the cwd. A silent misfire (running from Downloads and copying the wrong files) is worse than a refusal.

2_install_path_resolution.change: Default install path is now derived from $PSScriptRoot (sibling of deploy/). USB-deployable: a script at E:\OrderGetItRight\deploy\deploy.ps1 defaults to E:\OrderGetItRight. The hardcoded C:\OrderGetItRight is gone. -InstallPath still overrides.

3_python_version_gate.change: Step 2 checks the Python version. Refuses to proceed with < 3.12 (the build uses PEP 695 syntax; 3.11 will load the source and crash on import). Throws, not warns.

4_pip_is_best_effort.change: Step 3 catches pip install failure. A failed package sets $DeployDegraded=$true; the closing banner says DEGRADED, not COMPLETE. A deploy that reports COMPLETE must be a deploy that actually completed.

5_tauri_default_off.change: Step 5 only invokes build-tauri.ps1 if $env:OGIR_BUILD_TAURI=1 AND -SkipTauri was not passed. Default: skipped (Tauri takes 2-5 minutes and is not part of the runtime path).

6_templated_launchers.change: Step 4 templates every .bat from $InstallPath and $PythonExe at write time. The previous hardcoded C:\OrderGetItRight in launcher bodies is gone. USB-relative launchers work on the host that ran the deploy.

7_verify_chain_final.change: Step 6 runs src.verify_chain in the real (non-dry-run) flow and inspects stdout for "RESULT: MATCH". On mismatch, the deploy is marked DEGRADED and the script exits 2 (not 0). A deploy that did not verify the chain is a deploy that did not deploy.

8_yes_flag.change: -Yes skips the confirmation prompt. Default: prompt before mutating. The -Yes flag is the unattended mode (operator double-clicks and walks away). The prompt is a second-line defence against typo install paths.

payload.note: A3 closed. The seed-on-POST gap was the residual foot-gun: the test that was supposed to close A3 (test_seed_facts_preserves_operator_facts_across_reseed) was failing because POST /api/facts did not call _ensure_seeded(). Modern FastAPI TestClient does not fire the lifespan handler before the first request, so the seed facts were missing on a fresh process. The first operator POST in a fresh process would land in a registry with no seed facts. Fix: POST /api/facts now calls _ensure_seeded() before adding the operator fact. _seed_facts_once() is guarded by , so this is safe -- it never wipes operator facts. Test also reinforced: forces a clean baseline, asserts seed categories are present before the operator add, asserts operator id is not a seed id, asserts re-seed does not duplicate, asserts second re-seed is idempotent. test_smoke.py 28/28 pass; full suite 76 pass + 1 skip (D5 E2E).

The use of artificial intelligence or AI by researchers to write their scientific papers is far from A-OK right now. Just look at what a research team recently described a in a correspondence to The Lancet —over a three-year period, 4,046 references in 2,810 published scientific journal articles had been completely fabricated. Most of these fabrications were presumably hallucinations by AI, which kind of makes you wonder what else in those papers may have been artificial as well.

By 2026 Approximately One In 277 Papers Had Presumably AI-Fabricated Citations
To conduct the review of what might have been generated by AI, the research team from Columbia University (Maxim Topaza, Nir Roguinb, Pallavi Guptab and Zhihong Zhanga) and the University of Eastern Finland (Laura-Maria Peltonen) turned to, well, AI. They developed an automated reference verification system. That’s because reviewing all 2,471,758 papers with 125,615,773 accompanying references from January 1, 2023, through February 18, 2026, that are in PubMed Central’s Open Access would have taken quite a bit of time without some computational help.

Comparing citations listed in the papers with actual bibliographic records helped identify and flag any discrepancies. The research team used even more AI—a large language model known as Claude 3.5 Haiku from Anthropic—to help go through everything that was flagged and separate the honest errors from the pure fabrications. Any reference that couldn’t be found databases like PubMed, Crossref, OpenAlex and Google Scholar was considered not fab and instead fabricated.

During the first year searched—2023—approximately one in 2828 papers had at least one fabricated reference. In just two years—in 2025— this had already jumped up to one in 458. Yikes. Then the first seven weeks of 2026, an even higher one in 277 paper ratio. That’s an over 12-fold increase in a relatively short amount of time.

One Paper Published in 2025 Had 60 Percent Of Its Citations Presumably AI-Fabricated
One of the papers that deserved a particularly big F—for fabrication—was published in 2025 in an open access oncology journal and covered ureteroileal anastomotic techniques. A whopping 60 percent (18 of the 30) of the references cited in the paper were fabricated. There were other examples of papers with significant proportions of references fabricated. A total of 246 different papers contained three or more fabricated references.

The research team also identified particular authors who cranked out multiple papers with fabricated references. For example, a pair of authors had 11 different papers in a single surgical journal in 2025 that had 15 fabricated references. The research team called out so-called “paper mills,” in general. Using AI Large Language Models Has A High Risk For Hallucinations
Now without talking specifically to the authors, it’s difficult to tell why these fabricated citations made it into their paper. Presumably, the authors didn’t do it for fun, as in let’s make up a scientific paper with Taylor Swift and Justin Bieber as co-authors. The suspicion is that most of the fabrications resulted from hallucinations from a specific type of AI: large language models or LLMs for short in case you don’t have time to say “arge anguage odels.”

Authors’ reply
We thank Anselm Jorda and 
Markus Zeitlinger for highlighting 
the important distinction between 
statistical non-inferiority, inferiority, 
and equivalence.
Our phase 3 zoliflodacin randomised 
controlled trial (RCT)1 was designed 
to demonstrate non-inferiority to the 
standard of care—ceftriaxone plus 
azithromycin—per US Food and Drug 
Administration (FDA) and European 
Medicines Agency guidance2,3 for 
treating uncomplicated urogenital 
gonorrhoea and not to demonstrate 
statistical equivalence. 
1782 
The study met its objective 
(estimated treatment difference 5·3%, 
95% CI 1·4–8·6), with the upper bound 
of the two-sided 95% CI remaining 
below the prespecified non-inferiority 
margin. In doing so, the study has 
demonstrated preservation of a 
clinically meaningful proportion of the 
established control effect, consistent 
with the constancy assumption 
underlying a non-inferiority trial design. 
Our trial is the largest RCT conducted 
for uncomplicated urogenital 
gonorrhoea to date. The inclusion of 
geographically and racially diverse 
populations with the highest disease 
burden—South Africa (46%) and 
Thailand (29%)—is a key strength.  
Direct comparisons with other 
contemporary trials should therefore 
be interpreted cautiously due to 
heterogeneity in study populations, 
endpoint definitions, analysis 
populations, and ascertainment 
methods.  Exploratory whole-genome 
sequencing further provides evidence 
of reinfection among this study 
population.4
Lastly, the favourable safety profile 
of zoliflodacin was generated from a 
safety population of sufficient size to 
characterise common and clinically 
relevant adverse events that, with 
demonstrated efficacy, supports the 
unrestricted indication for use following 
FDA review.5  To echo the sentiment of 
Jorda and Zeitlinger, safety differences 
might also guide drug choice in 
individual patients when comparing oral 
and parenteral treatment strategies.
These data collectively reinforce, 
for the time being, the sustained high 
efficacy of ceftriaxone-based regimens 
in the regions where the studies were 
conducted, and the potential value 
of new treatment options beyond 
point estimates of efficacy—including 
route of administration, resistance 
mitigation, and patient acceptability—
amid the rising threat of global 
antimicrobial resistance.6

that ibrutinib–rituximab can reach 
chemotherapy-free disease control 
in older patients with mantle-cell 
lymphoma who were not eligible 
for transplantation. The ENRICH 
trial represents a pivotal advance, 
yet its findings invite refinement 
for broader clinical practice. First, 
the absence of minimal residual 
disease (MRD) monitoring reduces 
the opportunity to identify patients 
who could safely discontinue Bruton 
tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibition once 
deep molecular remission is reached. 
MRD-guided or circulating tumour 
DNA (ctDNA)-guided discontinuation 
could reduce cumulative exposure, 
thereby lessening toxicological 
risk, improving adherence, and 
optimising health-care resources.2 
Second, long-term indefinite 
ibrutinib therapy might not align with 
geriatric oncology principles, where 
multimorbidity, pharmacodynamic 
variability, and cumulative organ 
stress are central concerns. Time
restricted, adaptive regimens guided 
by MRD or imaging biomarkers could 
maintain efficacy while minimising 
chronic exposure and drug–drug 
interactions.3 Third, the observed 
cardiotoxicity—atrial fibrillation 
and cardiac deaths in approximately 
5–7% of participants—highlights 
the need for toxicology-informed 
pharmacovigilance, such as baseline 
cardiac biomarkers, structured rhythm 
monitoring, and proactive cardio
oncology collaboration.3,4 Integrating 
pharmacologic toxicology with 
molecular response profiling (eg, MRD 
or ctDNA) could yield an exposure
response–toxicity framework or 
a therapeutic monitoring index, 
balancing biological remission with 
systemic tolerance. Lastly, short
course chemoimmunotherapy 
induction followed by BTK-inhibitor 
maintenance could offer a pragmatic 
and globally applicable compromise, 
maintaining remission depth while 
potentially reducing long-term 
cardiovascular and systemic toxicity.5

Authors’ reply
We thank Gang Lv and colleagues for 
the response to our study.1 We agree 
that minimal residual disease (MRD) 
monitoring could help to optimise the 
treatment of mantle-cell lymphoma 
with ibrutinib and other Bruton tyrosine 
kinase (BTK) inhibitors. However, 
no study comparing outcomes of 
continuous use of BTK inhibitors 
versus an MRD-driven approach has yet 
been reported. Currently, continuous 
therapy with BTK inhibitors remains 
the standard of care in most first-line 
mantle-cell lymphoma studies.2,3
MRD was performed as an 
experimental endpoint in the ENRICH 
trial using a novel flow cytometric panel, 
and results will be published in a future 
manuscript, but MRD results were not 
used to inform treatment decisions.
In low-risk mantle-cell lymphoma, 
a single-arm study enrolling selected 
patients at low risk has demonstrated 
that cessation of continuous BTK 
inhibitor therapy might be possible 
and can be associated with favourable 
outcomes, but it is not yet clear 
how these results compare with 
chemotherapy approaches in this 
group of patients.4 Ongoing studies 
are assessing the role of MRD
directed treatment interruptions 
while receiving first-line BTK inhibitor 
treatment for mantle-cell lymphoma.5
We agree that the optimal first-line 
treatment for patients with mantle-cell 
lymphoma requires further refinement, 
and that combined chemotherapy plus 
BTK-inhibitor treatment might benefit 
patients, particularly those with high risk 
features such as high Ki67 and blastoid 
status.2 By contrast, chemotherapy-free 
combinations of rituximab and anti
CD20 antibody appear highly effective 
in patients with low-risk mantle-cell 
lymphoma.5,6 Future studies will refine 
novel treatment strategies to improve 
outcomes of patients with high-risk 
mantle-cell lymphoma for whom new 
approaches are required.1

the important distinction between

of the two-sided 95% CI remaining

demonstrated preservation of a 
clinically meaningful proportion of the 
established control effect, consistent 
with the constancy assumption 
underlying a non-inferiority trial design.

for uncomplicated urogenital 
gonorrhoea to date. The inclusion of 
geographically and racially diverse 
populations with the highest disease 
burden—South Africa (46%) and 
Thailand (29%)—is a key strength.

contemporary trials should therefore 
be interpreted cautiously due to 
heterogeneity in study populations, 
endpoint definitions, analysis

sequencing further provides evidence 
of reinfection among this study

conducted, and the potential value 
of new treatment options beyond

route of administration, resistance 
mitigation, and patient acceptability—
amid the rising threat of global

We thank Gang Lv and colleagues for 
the response to our study.1 We agree 
that minimal residual disease (MRD) 
monitoring could help to optimise the 
treatment of mantle-cell lymphoma 
with ibrutinib and other Bruton tyrosine 
kinase (BTK) inhibitors. However, 
no study comparing outcomes of 
continuous use of BTK inhibitors 
versus an MRD-driven approach has yet 
been reported. Currently, continuous 
therapy with BTK inhibitors remains 
the standard of care in most first-line 
mantle-cell lymphoma studies.2,3
MRD was performed as an 
experimental endpoint in the ENRICH 
trial using a novel flow cytometric panel, 
and results will be published in a future 
manuscript, but MRD results were not 
used to inform treatment decisions.
In low-risk mantle-cell lymphoma, 
a single-arm study enrolling selected 
patients at low risk has demonstrated 
that cessation of continuous BTK 
inhibitor therapy might be possible 
and can be associated with favourable 
outcomes, but it is not yet clear 
how these results compare with 
chemotherapy approaches in this 
group of patients.4 Ongoing studies 
are assessing the role of MRD
directed treatment interruptions 
while receiving first-line BTK inhibitor 
treatment for mantle-cell lymphoma.5
We agree that the optimal first-line 
treatment for patients with mantle-cell 
lymphoma requires further refinement, 
and that combined chemotherapy plus 
BTK-inhibitor treatment might benefit 
patients, particularly those with high risk 
features such as high Ki67 and blastoid 
status.2 By contrast, chemotherapy-free 
combinations of rituximab and anti
CD20 antibody appear highly effective 
in patients with low-risk mantle-cell 
lymphoma.5,6 Future studies will refine 
novel treatment strategies to improve 
outcomes of patients with high-risk 
mantle-cell lymphoma for whom new 
approaches are required.1

Offline: Climate and health—time to step up our activism
It is official: global warming is accelerating. In a paper 
published in Geophysical Research Letters in March, 2026, 
Grant Foster and Stefan Rahmstorf strip out the noise 
of natural variability in temperature measurements and 
conclude “with over 98% confidence” that planetary 
warming has speeded up since 2015. They call this 
acceleration “large and significant”. Why is it taking 
place? They speculate that reductions in air pollution 
might have diminished atmospheric cooling aerosols. 
Their conclusion is unusually blunt for a scientific paper:

*
As the world boils, progress on climate action stalls. In 
the 2026 Europe report of the Lancet Countdown on 
health and climate change, published this month in The 
Lancet Public Health, the news is bleak. European countries 
have experienced increases in direct (eg, heat exposure) 
and indirect (eg, infectious diseases) effects of warming. 
Europe recorded increases in heat-attributable mortality 
between 2015–24 compared with 1991–2000. Health 
warnings about extreme heat increased, as did time 
deemed unsafe for light or moderate physical activity 
during especially hot days. Food insecurity worsened. 
Outbreaks of Aedes-borne arboviruses rose. The pollen 
season lengthened. Despite these measurable harms, 
governments continue to give fossil-fuel industries a 
free pass. Annual fossil-fuel subsidies hit a new high 
in 2023. The good news is that renewable energy is 
contributing more to European electricity supplies—21·5% 
in 2023 compared with 8·4% in 2016. And clean energy 
investments are rising. But the Lancet Europe Countdown 
describes a disturbing trend: a decline in engagement 
about the health effects of climate change by politicians, 
business leaders, media, and the public. Health is still 
insufficiently prioritised in debates about climate action. 
As the Europe Countdown notes, “the climate and health 
intersection is nearly absent from parliamentary debates, 
www.thelancet.com   Vol 407   May 9, 2026 
social media strategies, and party communications, 
reflecting persistent policy silos”. This “engagement gap” 
is the most immediate challenge facing Europe’s climate 
and health community. Partly, it reflects political and 
public anxiety about cost-of-living pressures, exacerbated 
by wars in Ukraine and the Middle East. Partly, it reflects 
hostility to climate policies, and even to climate science, 
from newly emerging right-of-centre populist political 
parties. This adverse geopolitical context should be a 
stimulus to activists to step up their advocacy and protest.
*
The scale of the challenge can seem overwhelming. 
In Radical Justice: Building the World We Need (2026), 
Nani Jansen Reventlow argues that the climate 
emergency has colonial origins: “The causes of the climate 
crisis and the drivers of climate injustice are rooted in 
racism, colonialism, and capitalism.” She is right that 
“marginalised groups are the ones who are bearing 
the brunt of the climate crisis in real time”. The Europe 
Countdown report recognises that fundamental disparity: 
“Climate change risks, vulnerabilities, and impacts are 
unevenly distributed across population groups and 
regions.” Reventlow also writes that Europe’s climate 
movement—“dominated by middle-class white people”—
is failing to challenge the status quo and failing to create 
space for a much broader and more diverse community 
of activists. “What we need is a genuine shift in the 
composition of these fields’ dominant players.” How 
should we proceed? Each of us, Reventlow suggests, needs 
to find our own way of being an activist. You do not have 
to get arrested and imprisoned. You do not have to throw 
paint at a building. You do not have to lie in the road. You 
can find something that you are good at and pursue your 
own path (in Reventlow’s case, as a lawyer, it is litigation). 
She writes that, “We need a tapestry of activism to make 
change.” That conclusion must also be the conclusion 
of this year’s Europe Countdown report. A “tapestry of 
activism” is the only way to fill an “engagement gap” that 
is paralysing progress. Reventlow quotes Farzana Khan, 
founder of Healing Justice London: “if it is ‘safe enough to 
try, good enough for now’, you should go for it.”

LATTICE_FRAMING updated to note F7-deep wiring. On the Selby real evidence: S0=625, K1=531.25, K2=312.5, sigma1=0.6 (doubled from total spec gap), sigma2=0.35 (hiked by 75% compliance gap). Lattice now returns DEFER (totalValue 463.9 < threshold 717.2) -- the honest answer that the option to pursue is out of the money on pure expected-value terms, even though the BBFB merit verdict is REJECT. This is the product-verdict vs claim-verdict separation the lattice is meant to provide.
payload.before: Lattice inputs S0/K1/K2/sigma1/sigma2 were hardcoded stylised defaults (S0=55, K1=18, K2=10, sigma1=0.3, sigma2=0.2). payload.after: specAccuracy LAW gate now uses spec_value_curve(spec_ratio): a symmetric Taguchi-quadratic V(x) = 1 - ((x - 1.0)/1.0)^2 clamped to [0,1], peak at x*=1.0 (spec measured == spec claimed), declines on BOTH sides. Veto threshold V_min = V(PERFORMANCE_FLOOR) = V(0.5) = 0.75, preserving the veto boundary by construction (spec_ratio < 0.5 still fails; spec_ratio > 1.5 also fails). Over-spec now caught: V(1.75) = 0.4375 < 0.75 = veto. FRUIT perf_score now uses the curved spec_value too (policy decision: the curve IS the honest spec value). efficiencyAdequacy still uses raw spec_ratio with EFFICIENCY_FLOOR (separate gate, different semantics). 3 new constants: SPEC_BEST_BAND_X_STAR=1.0, SPEC_VALUE_WIDTH_W=1.0, SPEC_VALUE_VETO_FLOOR=0.75. 7 regression tests: boundary preserved (0.5 passes), under-spec vetoed (0.4 fails), peak at 1.0 (V=1.0), over-spec declines (1.75 fails, 1.5 passes at boundary), Selby still vetoed by warranty not spec, determinism (same input = same output). Research report at 04_Validation/DIMINISHING_RETURNS_RESEARCH_2026-07-19.md with primary-source citations (Taguchi 1986, Pratt 1964, EQ-5D, MAPS, ALDVMM). Path A (S-QoL/SWB layer) rejected: calibration irreducibly subjective, does not gate any decision, U(S) monotone cannot produce best-band.
payload.before: specAccuracy LAW gate used a hard floor: spec_ratio >= PERFORMANCE_FLOOR (0.5). Binary pass/fail with no diminishing-returns behaviour. FRUIT perf_score used raw spec_ratio linearly. Over-spec (specMeasured > specClaimed) passed with no penalty -- a product claiming 100 units and delivering 200 was scored as 'perfect'. The BBFB engine detected 'wing falls off' (total spec failure) but could not detect 'story of own demise' (over-spec dishonesty) or grade value on a curve.
files_changed: 02_Technical/src/engines/bbfb_engine.py:46-87 (spec_value_curve function), 129 (LAW specAccuracy uses curve), 176 (FRUIT perf_score uses curve)
payload.test_result: 227 passed, 1 skipped, 1 warning (7 new F7-SPEC tests; all existing tests unchanged including Selby validation run)
payload.validation_notes: The veto boundary is preserved by construction (V_min = V(PERFORMANCE_FLOOR)), not by re-test. The Selby case still vetoes on warrantyAdequacy, not specAccuracy (the research corrected the brief's wrong validation premise). The curve is pure math: no random, no optimisation, no third-party packages. Same input = same output on any host (PYTHONHASHSEED=0). This is the 'best band for buck / diminishing returns' behaviour the operator asked for, built on the Taguchi quadratic loss function (Taguchi 1986, Introduction to Quality Engineering).

CHAIN_OPERATOR_ID='OGIR-OPERATOR' is used in vault_io integrity_digest and orchestrator seal payloads — the shareable chain blocks. New blocks from this point forward carry OGIR-OPERATOR, not the operator's real name. Old blocks (1-20775) still carry the old operator identity in the integrity_digest and cannot be changed (append-only). The chain still verifies — the hash is over the canonical JSON payload, so the operator field change is transparent to the Merkle chain verification (it recomputes from the stored payload, not from the constant). Legal documents still use the real name. The indicator-driven decision: LAW gate (append-only + shareable + personal data = VETO risk) produced the pseudonymisation. GRACE: the legal documents still need the real name, so the split preserves both. FRUIT: the chain is shareable without leaking identity; the legal output is still signed by the real operator.
